'''Thomas Andrew Lehrer''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|l|ɛər|ər|audio=en-us-Lehrer.ogg}}; April 9, 1928 – July 26, 2025) was an American musician and mathematician. He recorded pithy, humorous, and often [[Music and politics|political songs]] that became popular in the 1950s and 1960s. His songs parodied popular musical forms, often with original melodies.

Lehrer's early performances dealt with non-topical subjects and [[dark humor]] in songs such as "[[Poisoning Pigeons in the Park]]". In the 1960s, he produced songs about timely social and political issues, particularly for the U.S. version of the television show ''[[That Was the Week That Was]]''. Lehrer quoted a friend's explanation: "Always predict the worst and you'll be hailed as a prophet."<ref>{{cite episode|last=Ford|first=Andrew|title=Tom Lehrer|series=The Music Show|transcript=Interview transcript|transcript-url=http://www.abc.net.au/radionational/programs/musicshow/tom-lehrer/3344656#transcript|date=July 8, 2006|station=[[Radio National]]|network=Australian Broadcasting Corporation}}</ref> In the early 1970s, Lehrer largely retired from public performance to devote his time to teaching mathematics and musical theater history at the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]].

==Early life==
[[File:Tom Lehrer in 1943 Loomiscellany.jpg|thumb|upright|Lehrer in [[Loomis Chaffee School|Loomis School]]'s 1943 yearbook]]

Thomas Andrew Lehrer was born in New York City on April 9, 1928, and grew up on [[Manhattan]]'s [[Upper East Side]].<ref name="Smith">{{cite news|last=Smith|first=Ben|title=Looking For Tom Lehrer, Comedy's Mysterious Genius|url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/bensmith/tom-lehrer|access-date=April 12, 2014|newspaper=[[BuzzFeed]]|date=April 9, 2014|author-link=Ben Smith (journalist)|archive-date=November 29, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211129061734/https://www.buzzfeed.com/bensmith/tom-lehrer|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{cite book|title=Celebrities in Hell|year=2002|publisher=ChelCpress|isbn=9781569802144|page=72|author=Warren Allen Smith|chapter=Tom Lehrer|quote=He responded: No one is more dangerous than someone who thinks he has The Truth. To be an atheist is almost as arrogant as to be a fundamentalist. But then again, I can get pretty arrogant.}}</ref> He was the son of Morris James Lehrer (1897–1986), a successful necktie designer, and Anna Lehrer (née Waller; 1905–1978) and older brother of Barry Waller Lehrer (1930–2007).<ref>{{Cite web|title=Spotlight: 1960s satirist Tom Lehrer resurfaces|url=https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/18835086.spotlight-1960s-satirist-tom-lehrer-resurfaces/|access-date=February 12, 2022|website=HeraldScotland|date=November 2020 |language=en|archive-date=February 12, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220212072525/https://www.heraldscotland.com/news/18835086.spotlight-1960s-satirist-tom-lehrer-resurfaces/|url-status=live}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|date=May 31, 2000|title=Tom Lehrer: An equal opportunity offender|url=https://www.jta.org/2000/05/31/lifestyle/tom-lehrer-an-equal-opportunity-offender|access-date=February 12, 2022|website=Jewish Telegraphic Agency|archive-date=February 12, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220212072523/https://www.jta.org/2000/05/31/lifestyle/tom-lehrer-an-equal-opportunity-offender|url-status=live}}</ref>{{efn|Lehrer's Harvard University friend [[Jeremy Bernstein]] wrote, "During the time I knew him, Lehrer spoke to me very little about his family. I had the feeling he was an only child, since he never spoke about any siblings... I am very familiar with the New York private high schools of that era, having attended one, so I know that anyone who went to [[Horace Mann School|Horace Mann]] must have been from a family that was comfortably well-off. I believe that his father manufactured ties... It was when he was fourteen that his parents got divorced."<ref name="Medium" />}} Lehrer told an interviewer that he recalled an idyllic childhood on [[Manhattan]]'s [[Upper West Side]] that included attending [[Broadway theatre|Broadway shows]] with his family and walking through [[Central Park]] day or night.<ref name="PBS">{{cite web |last1=Flaccus |first1=Gillian |last2=Rogers |first2=John |date=July 27, 2025 |title=Tom Lehrer, mathematician and singer-songwriter known for colorful satire, dies at 97 |url=https://www.pbs.org/newshour/arts/tom-lehrer-mathematician-and-singer-songwriter-known-for-colorful-satire-dies-at-97 |publisher=[[PBS]] |access-date=September 6, 2025}}</ref> He and his family were ethnically [[Jews|Jewish]], following a generally secular lifestyle that included attending [[Hebrew school|Jewish Sunday school]] but also [[Jews and Christmas|celebrating Christmas]]; he remarked that his ties to Judaism were "more to do with the delicatessen than the synagogue (...) and 'God' was primarily an expletive(.)"<ref>{{Cite web |last=Alt Miller |first=Yvette |date=2025-07-28 |title=Tom Lehrer and His Irreverent Songs |url=https://aish.com/tom-lehrer-and-his-irreverent-songs/ |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=Aish.com |language=en-US}}</ref> As a child, he loved logic puzzles and math.<ref name="Bianculli">{{cite web |last=Bianculli |first=David |author-link=David Bianculli |date=August 1, 2025 |title=Remembering composer and musical satirist Tom Lehrer |url=https://www.npr.org/2025/08/01/nx-s1-5486787/remembering-composer-and-musical-satirist-tom-lehrer |publisher=[[NPR]] |access-date=September 6, 2025}}</ref> He began taking classical piano lessons at the age of seven but was more interested in the popular music of the age. Eventually, his mother sent him to a piano teacher who taught him how to play the [[Broadway theatre|Broadway]] show tunes he loved.<ref name="Liner notes">Liner notes, ''Songs & More Songs By Tom Lehrer'', Rhino Records, 1997.</ref> At this early age, he began writing [[show tune]]s, which eventually helped him as a satirical composer and writer in his years of lecturing at [[Harvard University]] and later at other universities.<ref>{{cite web|title=Tom Lehrer: The Political Musician That Wasn't|author=Jeremy Mazner|url=http://www.casualhacker.net/tom.lehrer/jmazner/lehrhtml.html|website=Casualhacker.net|access-date=October 25, 2019|archive-date=September 30, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190930102441/http://www.casualhacker.net/tom.lehrer/jmazner/lehrhtml.html|url-status=live}}</ref>

Lehrer attended the [[Horace Mann School]] in [[Riverdale, New York|Riverdale]], part of [[the Bronx]] borough of New York.<ref name="Smith"/><ref name="Toobin">{{cite web |first=Jeffrey R |last=Toobin |author-link=Jeffrey Toobin |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1981/11/9/tom-lehrer-pbrbumors-to-the-contrary/ |title=Tom Lehrer |work=The Harvard Crimson |date=November 9, 1981 |access-date=April 14, 2012 |archive-date=August 7, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130807114423/http://www.thecrimson.com/article/1981/11/9/tom-lehrer-pbrbumors-to-the-contrary/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He also attended [[Camp Androscoggin]], both as a camper and a counselor.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.summercore.com/ronin |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120201005628/http://www.summercore.com/ronin/ |archive-date=February 1, 2012 |title=The Elements by Tom Lehrer |access-date=May 23, 2013}}</ref> [[Stephen Sondheim]] had Tom Lehrer as a camp counselor.<ref>{{cite magazine |last1=Gopnik |first1=Adam |author1-link=Adam Gopnik |title=The Rules of Rhyme |url=https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2022/05/30/the-rules-of-rhyme-daniel-levin-becker-whats-good-notes-on-rap-and-language |access-date=July 28, 2025 |magazine=[[The New Yorker]] |date=May 23, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250126122144/https://www.newyorker.com/magazine/2022/05/30/the-rules-of-rhyme-daniel-levin-becker-whats-good-notes-on-rap-and-language |archive-date=January 26, 2025}}</ref><ref name="Bernstein"/>

Lehrer was considered a child prodigy and skipped two grades.<ref>Flaccus, Gillian, "[https://apnews.com/article/tom-lehrer-son-satirist-mathematician-dies-9caa7ee01faf4fbfb793d7ba984c179d Tom Lehrer, song satirist and mathematician, dies at 97] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727214036/https://apnews.com/article/tom-lehrer-son-satirist-mathematician-dies-9caa7ee01faf4fbfb793d7ba984c179d |date=July 27, 2025 }}", The Associated Press, July 27, 2025</ref> After graduation from [[Loomis Chaffee School|Loomis School]], at the age of 15 he entered [[Harvard College]], where one of his professors was [[Irving Kaplansky]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://mtarchive.blogspot.com/2013/09/a-song-about-pi.html|title=MTArchive: A Song about Pi|website=Mtarchive.blogspot.com|date=September 22, 2013|access-date=October 25, 2019|archive-date=October 25, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191025142856/http://mtarchive.blogspot.com/2013/09/a-song-about-pi.html|url-status=live}}</ref><ref name="Kaplansky" /><ref name="Smith" /> As an undergraduate student at Harvard, he began to write [[comic song]]s to entertain his friends, including "[[Fight Fiercely, Harvard]]". 

A fellow student and friend,{{efn|Bernstein said that Lehrer's wit was evident even in his teens. "Lehrer and I sometimes had lunch together in the graduate dining room. On one occasion, a student waiter dropped a tray filled with silverware and dishes, with a resounding crash. 'They are playing our song,' Lehrer commented." Bernstein wrote in 2020, "From time to time, we email each other. We once reminisced about a math graduate student who was known for his obnoxiousness. He was so obnoxious that to find a practical unit of obnoxiousness, you had to use a millionth of his actual name."<ref name="Medium" />}} the physicist [[Jeremy Bernstein]], recalled that he was told to organize a luncheon entertainment for the seniors graduating in 1951.<ref name="Medium">{{cite web |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |author-link=Jeremy Bernstein |date=Jul 10, 2020 |title=The mathematical and musical life of Tom Lehrer |url=https://medium.com/history-uncut/the-mathematical-and-musical-life-of-tom-lehrer-a1c1e903dc67 |publisher=Oxford Academic, [[Oxford University Press]] |work=Medium |access-date=September 6, 2025}}</ref> He knew only two entertainers, Lehrer and [[Al Capp]], both of whom agreed. Lehrer ("and a small group of co-conspirators," Bernstein wrote) performed his songs as ''The Physical Revue'' for Harvard's physics department then and again in 1952.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://ww3.haverford.edu/physics/songs/lehrer/physrev.htm |title=The Physical Revue, by Tom Lehrer |publisher=Ww3.haverford.edu |date=October 22, 2003 |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=September 23, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923032040/https://ww3.haverford.edu/physics/songs/lehrer/physrev.htm |url-status=live }}</ref> Bernstein said, "This performance had remarkable consequences for Lehrer. Capp had a weekly radio program, and Lehrer became a fixture. I think that this was the first time he had been let loose on the general public, although the program only lasted four weeks."<ref name="Medium" /> The revue was revived by Lehrer in 1993 as ''Songs of the Physical Revue'' – a special performance for the [[American Physical Society]] to commemorate the centenary of their journal, the ''[[Physical Review]]''.<ref>{{citation |date=April 20, 1993 |title=Physicists Celebrate Unintelligible Journal |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/04/20/science/physicists-celebrate-unintelligible-journal.html |access-date=July 28, 2025 |language=en |newspaper=The New York Times |archive-date=May 29, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230529085602/https://www.nytimes.com/1993/04/20/science/physicists-celebrate-unintelligible-journal.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

==Academic and military career==
[[File:Tom Lehrer in The Harvard Album 1947–1948.jpg|thumb|upright|Lehrer in [[Harvard University]]'s 1947–1948 yearbook]]
[[File:Tom Lehrer, Robert H. Welker, David Z. Robinson, and Lewis M. Branscomb perform on Arbor Day at Harvard University, 1951.jpg|thumb|upright|(From left) Lehrer, Robert H. Welker, David Z. Robinson, and [[Lewis M. Branscomb]] perform a hymn for the Harvard Spring rites on Arbor Day, 1951. The quartet performed songs for ''The Physical Revue''.]]
Lehrer graduated from [[Harvard University|Harvard]] with a [[Bachelor of Arts]] in mathematics, ''[[magna cum laude]]'',<ref>{{Cite news |last=Toobin |first=Jeffrey R. |author-link=Jeffrey Toobin |date=November 9, 1981 |title=Tom Lehrer |work=The Harvard Crimson |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1981/11/9/tom-lehrer-pbrbumors-to-the-contrary/ |access-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201022215849/https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1981/11/9/tom-lehrer-pbrbumors-to-the-contrary/ |url-status=live }}</ref> in 1946.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://dmdb.org/lehrer/bio.html |title=Tom Lehrer Biography |publisher=Dmdb.org |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=October 31, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20151031114929/http://dmdb.org/lehrer/bio.html |url-status=live }}</ref> At Harvard, he was the roommate of the Canadian theologian [[Robert Crouse]].<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Burton |first=Anthony |author-link=Tony Burton (bishop) |date=Easter 2011 |title=In Memoriam: The Revd. Dr. Robert Crouse |url=http://prayerbook.ca/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/PBSC-Newsletter-Easter-2011.pdf |magazine=The Prayer Book Society of Canada Newsletter |page=1 |access-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-date=August 24, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160824054739/http://prayerbook.ca/wp-content/uploads/2014/03/PBSC-Newsletter-Easter-2011.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> He received his [[Master of Arts|MA]] degree the next year and was inducted into [[Phi Beta Kappa]].<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lynch |first=Peter |date=September 17, 2018 |title=Tom Lehrer: a comical, musical, mathematical genius |language=en |newspaper=The Irish Times |url=https://www.irishtimes.com/news/science/tom-lehrer-a-comical-musical-mathematical-genius-1.3632032 |access-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-date=October 20, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201020012058/https://www.irishtimes.com/news/science/tom-lehrer-a-comical-musical-mathematical-genius-1.3632032 |url-status=live }}</ref> He later taught mathematics and other classes at [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology|MIT]], Harvard, [[Wellesley College|Wellesley]], and the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]].<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-may-26-ca-34112-story.html |title=Tom Lehrer's Playful Satire Still Delivers a Musical Punch |first=Richard |last=Cromelin |newspaper=Los Angeles Times |date=May 26, 2000 |access-date=October 23, 2019 |archive-date=October 23, 2019 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20191023135728/https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2000-may-26-ca-34112-story.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Lehrer remained in Harvard's doctoral program for several years, taking time also for his musical career.<ref name="Boulware">{{cite web |url=https://archives.sfweekly.com/sanfrancisco/that-was-the-wit-that-was/Content?oid=2138455 |title=That Was the Wit That Was |first=Jack |last=Boulware |work=[[SF Weekly]] |date=April 19, 2000 |access-date=July 27, 2025 |archive-date=October 25, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211025111743/https://archives.sfweekly.com/sanfrancisco/that-was-the-wit-that-was/Content?oid=2138455&showFullText=true |url-status=live }}</ref> "I spent many, many years satisfying all the requirements, as many years as possible, and I started on the [[Thesis#United States|thesis]]," he once said. "But I just wanted to be a grad student, it's a wonderful life. That's what I wanted to be, and unfortunately, you can't be a Ph.D. and a grad student at the same time."<ref name="PBS" />

Lehrer reportedly worked briefly as a researcher with [[Stan Ulam]] at the [[Los Alamos Scientific Laboratory]] for two months in 1952.<ref>{{cite news |title=Music: Time Out from Thinking |url=https://time.com/archive/6797704/music-time-out-from-thinking/ |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[TIME.com]] |date=January 4, 1954 |language=en}}</ref><ref>Los Alamos Daily Post, August 14, 2025, ''Pages Of Our History: Remembering Tom Lehrer'', access date October 25, 2025</ref>

In 1953, Lehrer left Harvard to work for Baird-Atomic, which made scientific and industrial instruments, including radiation detection and [[spectroscopy]].<ref>{{cite web |title=Lehrer, Tom (1928—2025) |url=https://www.encyclopedia.com/media/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/lehrer-tom-1928 |website=[[Encyclopedia.com]] |access-date=July 27, 2025 |archive-date=May 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250512222817/https://www.encyclopedia.com/media/encyclopedias-almanacs-transcripts-and-maps/lehrer-tom-1928 |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=ATOMIC ENERGY: The Powerhouse |url=https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,937107-1,00.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |work=[[TIME.com]] |date=January 12, 1959 |archive-date=April 10, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230410204635/https://content.time.com/time/subscriber/article/0,33009,937107-1,00.html |url-status=live }}</ref><!-- https://www.cia.gov/readingroom/document/cia-rdp81b00878r001300200013-6 -->

Lehrer was [[Conscription in the United States|drafted]] into the [[U.S. Army]] in 1955.{{efn|Bernstein wrote, "Lehrer was still a graduate student and had published at least one technical mathematics paper. But in 1955, he was drafted into the army for two years, part of which he spent at Los Alamos and most of which he spent at the [[National Security Agency]] in Washington. I never found out what he did at these places. He once told me that NSA stood for No Such Agency. My guess is that it was probably [[Cryptanalysis|codebreaking]]. One of our Harvard math professors, [[Andrew M. Gleason|Andrew Gleason]], had spent the war cracking Japanese codes. It was after his military service that Lehrer's career as a touring performer took off."<ref name="Medium" />}} He served until 1957, working at the [[National Security Agency]] (NSA). Lehrer once stated that he invented the [[Jello shot]] during this time, as a means of circumventing the base's ban on alcoholic beverages.<ref name="Boulware"/> 
Despite holding a master's degree in an era when American conscripts often lacked high school diplomas, Lehrer served as an [[enlisted soldier]], achieving the rank of [[Specialist (rank)#Specialist (1955–present)|specialist third class]], which he described as being a "corporal [[Minister without portfolio|without portfolio]]".<ref>Monologue self-introduction on ''[[Tom Lehrer Revisited]]''.</ref> These experiences became fodder for songs, such as "The Wild West is Where I Want to Be" and "It Makes a Fellow Proud to Be a Soldier".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://m.youtube.com/watch?v=1U2fpzw4qNI | archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211118/1U2fpzw4qNI| archive-date=November 18, 2021 | url-status=live|title=The Wild West is Where I Want to Be: spoken introduction |first=Tom |last=Lehrer |work=[[The Remains of Tom Lehrer]] |date=May 23, 2000 |access-date=August 15, 2018}}{{cbignore}}</ref> In 2020 Lehrer publicly revealed that he had been assigned to the NSA; since the mere fact of the NSA's existence was classified at the time, Lehrer found himself in the position of implicitly using nuclear weapons work as a cover story for something more sensitive.<ref>{{Cite book|last=Bernstein|first=Jeremy|author-link=Jeremy Bernstein|title=Quantum Profiles|publisher=Oxford University Press|year=2020|edition=2|isbn=978-0-190-05686-5}}</ref>

In 1960, Lehrer returned to full-time mathematics studies at Harvard.<ref name="Toobin"/> From 1962 he taught mathematics in the [[political science]] department at [[MIT]] in [[Cambridge, Massachusetts]].<ref>{{cite encyclopedia|url=http://findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_g1epc/is_bio/ai_2419200709/ |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20050518090240/http://www.findarticles.com/p/articles/mi_g1epc/is_bio/ai_2419200709 |url-status=usurped |archive-date=May 18, 2005 |title=Tom Lehrer |last=Longley |first=Eric |work=St. James Encyclopedia of Pop Culture |encyclopedia=[[St. James Encyclopedia of Popular Culture]] }}</ref> In 1965 he gave up on his mathematics dissertation on [[Mode (statistics)|modes]] in statistics, after working on it intermittently for 15 years.<ref name="Smith"/>

Over time, Lehrer grew tired of shoveling snow in the harsh Cambridge winters; he already knew he liked California's Bay Area.<ref name="Medium" /><ref name="Tromba" /> He contacted botany professor [[Kenneth V. Thimann]], provost of [[Crown College, University of California, Santa Cruz]], and suggested teaching courses in [[Musical theatre|musical theater]]. Since Crown was science-oriented, Thimann asked mathematician [[Anthony Joseph Tromba]], who had been at Harvard and knew of Lehrer's musical antics, to find him a position at humanities-heavy [[Cowell College]] instead. Tromba sold Lehrer to the Fellowship Committee: "No one on the committee had heard of Tom. So I had to convince them that it was a great idea... We had Ph.D.s in music and art history who did scholarly work. But Cowell also wanted to have practicing artists to give students actual meaningful contact with them. Rather than just writing papers about [[Michelangelo]], let's have Michelangelo here—and why not?"<ref name="Tromba">{{cite web |last=Peña |first=Mike |date=August 1, 2025 |title=Why math and musical prodigy Tom Lehrer was so well-suited for young UC Santa Cruz. The uncomfortably famous satirical songwriter taught as a Cowell College fellow from 1972 to 2001 |url=https://news.ucsc.edu/2025/08/tom-lehrer/ |publisher=[[University of California, Santa Cruz|UC Santa Cruz]] |work=News |quote=Lehrer was officially a Lecturer in American Studies, not mathematics. In his primary course, The American Musical, Lehrer explored classics like ''[[My Fair Lady]]'', ''[[Guys and Dolls]]'', ''[[Camelot (musical)|Camelot]]'', and ''[[The King and I]]''. |access-date=September 6, 2025}}</ref> So in 1972, Lehrer joined the faculty of the [[University of California, Santa Cruz]] (UCSC). Tromba said that Lehrer was officially a "Lecturer in American Studies,"<ref name="Tromba" /> not mathematics, though he taught two introductory classes, "The Nature of Mathematics" and "Mathematics in the Social Sciences," to liberal arts majors—"Math for Tenors", according to Lehrer. He occasionally performed songs in his lectures.<ref name="Kaplansky">Lehrer performance excerpt, {{cite web|url=https://archive.org/details/lehrer |title=Irving "Kaps" Kaplansky's 80th Birthday Celebration|date=1997 |access-date=October 27, 2015}}</ref> 

In 2001, Lehrer taught his last mathematics class, on the topic of [[infinity]], and retired from academia.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://spectator.org/33723_whatever-happened-tom-lehrer/ |title=Whatever Happened to Tom Lehrer? |work=The American Spectator |date=April 1, 2013 |first=Alan |last=Reynolds |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=May 18, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160518145545/http://spectator.org/33723_whatever-happened-tom-lehrer/ |url-status=live }}</ref> He remained in the area, maintaining homes in both Santa Cruz and Cambridge.<ref name="Severo" /> In 2003 Lehrer confirmed he still "h[ung] out" around UCSC.<ref name="SMH">{{cite news|date=March 1, 2003|title=Stop clapping, this is serious|newspaper=smh.com.au|url=https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/art-and-design/stop-clapping-this-is-serious-20030301-gdgcoz.html|access-date=October 27, 2015|archive-date=August 14, 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180814184002/https://www.smh.com.au/entertainment/art-and-design/stop-clapping-this-is-serious-20030301-gdgcoz.html|url-status=live}}</ref> Mike Peña of UCSC said in 2025, "Lehrer's reputation matched UC Santa Cruz's creative and irreverent spirit; and his talents played perfectly into the campus's original intent to elevate the humanities and foster deeper connections between scholarship and society... Lehrer taught at UC Santa Cruz until 2001 and last came here about five years ago. His cultural contributions are so woven into the American fabric that they ensure his place as one of the most beloved educators ever to teach at our campus."<ref name="Tromba" />

==Musical career==
===Style and influences===

| above            = When You Are Old&nbsp;and&nbsp;Gray

Lehrer was mainly influenced by [[musical theater]]. According to [[Gerald Nachman (journalist)|Gerald Nachman]]'s book ''Seriously Funny'',<ref>{{cite book |last1= Nachman |first1=Gerald |author-link1= Gerald Nachman (journalist) |title=Seriously Funny: The Rebel Comedians of the 1950s and 1960s|url=https://archive.org/details/seriouslyfunnyre00nach |url-access= registration |location=New York, NY |publisher=Pantheon Books |publication-date=2003 |page=[https://archive.org/details/seriouslyfunnyre00nach/page/659 659] |isbn=  9780375410307 <!-- 0375410309 --> |oclc=50339527  |year= 2004}}</ref> the [[Broadway musical]] ''[[Let's Face It!]]'' made an early and lasting impression on him. Lehrer's style consists of [[Parody music|parodying]] various forms of [[popular song]]. For example, his appreciation of [[list song]]s led him to write "[[The Elements (song)|The Elements]]", which lists the [[chemical element]]s to the tune of [[Gilbert and Sullivan]]'s "[[Major-General's Song]]" from ''[[The Pirates of Penzance]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://gasdisc.oakapplepress.com/mdlehrer.htm|title=Tom Lehrer's 'The Elements' and 'Clementine' (1959) The Gilbert and Sullivan Discography|access-date=November 18, 2023|archive-date=October 12, 2007|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071012064103/http://www.cris.com/~oakapple/gasdisc/mdlehrer.htm|url-status=usurped}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ball |first=Philip |date=2025-07-29 |title=Scientists mourn Tom Lehrer — nerdiest of singer-songwriters |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/d41586-025-02417-w |journal=Nature |language=en |doi=10.1038/d41586-025-02417-w |pmid=40730929 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

{{blockquote
|text=He gave his first public concert as a third-year graduate student, at the [[Memorial Hall (Harvard University)#Sanders Theatre|Sanders Theatre]] in 1950.
|author=[[Jeremy Bernstein]]<ref name="Bernstein">{{cite news |last1=Bernstein |first1=Jeremy |author1-link=Jeremy Bernstein |title=They're playing our song |url=https://www.lrb.co.uk/blog/2021/october/they-re-playing-our-song |archive-url=https://archive.today/20250728001255/https://www.lrb.co.uk/blog/2021/october/they-re-playing-our-song |archive-date=28 July 2025 |access-date=28 July 2025 |work=LRB Blog, [[London Review of Books]] |date=13 October 2021 |language=en}}</ref>
}}

In author and [[Boston University]] professor [[Isaac Asimov]]'s second autobiographical volume, ''In Joy Still Felt'', Asimov recounted seeing Lehrer perform in a [[Boston]] nightclub on October 9, 1954. Lehrer sang a song about Jim getting it from Louise, and Sally from Jim, "...&nbsp;and after a while you gathered the 'it' was [[venereal disease]]. Suddenly, as the combinations grew more grotesque, you realized he was satirizing every known [[sexual perversion|perversion]] without using a single naughty phrase. It was clearly unsingable outside a nightclub." Asimov also recalled a song that dealt with the [[Boston subway]] system, making use of the stations leading into town from Harvard, observing that the local subject-matter rendered the song useless for general distribution. Lehrer subsequently granted Asimov permission to print the lyrics to "The Subway Song" in his book. "I haven't gone to nightclubs often," said Asimov, "but of all the times I have gone, it was on this occasion that I had by far the best time."<ref>Asimov, Isaac, ''In Joy Still Felt: The Autobiography of Isaac Asimov, 1954–1978''. Garden City, New York: Doubleday, 1980, p. 15.</ref>

===Recordings===

| above            = We Will All Go Together When&nbsp;We&nbsp;Go

| embed        = yes
}}

Lehrer was encouraged by the success of his performances, so he paid $15 ({{Inflation|US|15|1953|fmt=eq}}) to record in a single one-hour session on January 22, 1953, at the [[Transradio Press Service|TransRadio]] studio on Boylston Street<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Seale |first1=Lisa A. |title='Falling Forward': Frost's and Stevens' Public Readings |journal=The Wallace Stevens Journal |date=2017 |volume=41 |issue=1 |pages=23–37 |jstor=26755425 |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/26755425 |access-date=July 28, 2025 |issn=0148-7132 |quote=on October 8, 1954, at Transradio Studio on Boylston Street in. Boston—under the auspices of the Woodberry Poetry Room (and its then curator Jack ...}}</ref> in Boston, ''[[Songs by Tom Lehrer]]''.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Zobel |first1=Hiller B. |title=Songs by Tom Lehrer; Transradio Records |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1953/5/29/songs-by-tom-lehrer-pas-the/ |access-date=July 28, 2025 |work=[[The Harvard Crimson]] |date=May 29, 1953 |archive-date=December 27, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221227004836/https://www.thecrimson.com/article/1953/5/29/songs-by-tom-lehrer-pas-the/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Publika |first1=Liz |title=The Mathematical Elements That Comprise the Awesome Satirical Songs of Tom Lehrer |url=https://www.artpublikamag.com/post/the-mathematical-elements-that-comprise-the-awesome-satirical-songs-of-tom-lehrer |website=ARTpublika Magazine |access-date=July 28, 2025 |language=en |date=December 1, 2020 |archive-date=April 28, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250428155537/https://www.artpublikamag.com/post/the-mathematical-elements-that-comprise-the-awesome-satirical-songs-of-tom-lehrer |url-status=live }}</ref> The initial pressing was 400 copies. Radio stations would not air his songs because of his controversial subjects, so he sold the album on campus at Harvard for $3, {{Inflation|US|3|1953|fmt=eq|cursign=$}}, while "several stores near the Harvard campus sold it for $3.50, taking only a minimal markup as a kind of community service. Newsstands on campus sold it for the same price."<ref name="Demento">{{Cite AV media |author=Dr. Demento |author-link=Dr. Demento |title=''"Too Many Facts About Tom Lehrer"'' |work=The Remains of Tom Lehrer |publisher=Warner Bros Records | medium=CD liner notes |year=2000}}</ref> After one summer, he started to receive mail orders from all parts of the country, as far away as San Francisco, after the ''[[San Francisco Chronicle]]'' wrote an article on the record.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Bernstein |first=Jeremy |author-link=Jeremy Bernstein |date=1984 |title=Out of My Mind: Tom Lehrer: Having Fun |url=https://www.jstor.org/stable/41211046 |journal=The American Scholar |volume=53 |issue=3 |pages=295–302 |issn=0003-0937 |jstor=41211046 |access-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-date=October 27, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201027051436/https://www.jstor.org/stable/41211046 |url-status=live }}</ref> Interest in his recordings spread by word of mouth. People played their records for friends, who then also wanted a copy.<ref name="Bessman">Jim Bessman. "Rhino Reissues Lehrer's Seminal 'Songs' Albums". ''[[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]''. June 21, 1997.</ref> Lehrer recalled, "Lacking exposure in the media, my songs spread slowly. Like [[herpes]], rather than [[ebola]]."<ref>Maslon, Laurence, ''Make Em Laugh: The Funny Business of America'', Hachette Book Group, 2008, pg. 81</ref>

The album included the macabre "I Hold Your Hand in Mine", the mildly risqué "Be Prepared", and "[[Lobachevsky (song)|Lobachevsky]]", regarding plagiarizing mathematicians. It became a [[Cult following|cult success]] by word of mouth, despite being self-published and without promotion. The limited distribution of the album led to a knock-off album by Jack "Eljan" (a pseudonym of Jack Nagel) being released in 1958 without Lehrer's approval, where some of the lyrics were mistranscribed.<ref name="Crazy College">{{cite web|url=http://www.crazycollege.org/lehrer.html|title=An Interview with Tom Lehrer|publisher=Crazy College|access-date=May 8, 2023|archive-date=May 8, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230508123320/http://www.crazycollege.org/lehrer.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Lehrer embarked on a series of concert tours and recorded a second album in 1959. He released the second album in two versions: the songs were the same, but ''[[More of Tom Lehrer]]'' was a studio recording and ''[[An Evening Wasted with Tom Lehrer]]'' was recorded live in concert. In 2013, Lehrer recalled the studio session for "Poisoning Pigeons in the Park", which referred to<!--the cited ref. doesn't say this--> the practice of controlling pigeons in Boston with [[strychnine]]-treated corn:<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Faulkner |first=Clarence |date=May 1, 1999 |title=As It Was in Region 5, 1949–1964 |url=https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1045&context=icwdmprobe |journal=The Probe |volume=200 |page=7 |via=DigitalCommons@University of Nebraska - Lincoln, "City-wide pigeon control in Boston, MA using strychnine-treated whole corn" |access-date=March 2, 2020 |archive-date=March 31, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200331095921/https://digitalcommons.unl.edu/cgi/viewcontent.cgi?article=1045&context=icwdmprobe |url-status=live }}</ref>

{{Blockquote|The copyist arrived at the last minute with the parts and passed them out to the band&nbsp;... And there was no title on it, and there was no lyrics.  And so they ran through it, "What a pleasant little waltz"&nbsp;... And the engineer said, {{"'}}Poisoning Pigeons in the Park,' take one," and the piano player said, "What?" and literally fell off the stool.<ref name="BBC 2013-04-06">{{cite web |title=Tom Lehrer at 85 |url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01rqb1w |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130407021530/http://www.bbc.co.uk/programmes/b01rqb1w |archive-date=April 7, 2013 |url-status=dead |publisher=[[BBC Radio 4]] |date=April 6, 2013 |access-date=September 24, 2019 |via=The [[Public Radio Exchange]] }} [https://beta.prx.org/stories/104334 Alt URL] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190925023544/https://beta.prx.org/stories/104334 |date=September 25, 2019 }}</ref>}}

===Touring===
[[File:Tom_Lehrer_has_become_an_honorary_student_in_the_Studenterforeningen_(Copenhagen_Student_Union).jpg|thumb|upright|Lehrer as an honorary member of the Copenhagen Student Union, 1967]]
Lehrer had a breakthrough in the United Kingdom on December 4, 1957, when the [[University of London]] awarded a [[doctor of music]] degree ''[[honoris causa]]'' to [[Princess Margaret]], and the public orator, Professor J. R. Sutherland, said it was "in the full knowledge that the Princess is a connoisseur of music and a performer of skill and distinction, her taste being catholic, ranging from Mozart to the [[Calypso music|calypso]] and from opera to the songs of Miss [[Beatrice Lillie]] and Tom Lehrer."<ref>{{cite book |title=East Africa and Rhodesia |year=1957 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=h64qAAAAMAAJ |page=493 |access-date=September 17, 2017 |archive-date=April 26, 2016 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160426165710/https://books.google.com/books?id=h64qAAAAMAAJ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/51200645/|title=The Kansas City Times from Kansas City, Missouri · Page 4|date=December 5, 1957|work=The Kansas City Times|agency=[[Associated Press]]|location=Kansas City, Missouri|page=4|access-date=February 29, 2016|archive-date=March 4, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304125752/https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/51200645/|url-status=live |via=[[Newspapers.com]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V7KVCLZuC58| archive-url=https://ghostarchive.org/varchive/youtube/20211118/V7KVCLZuC58| archive-date=November 18, 2021 | url-status=live|title=British Pathé, quoted only "from Mozart to calypso"| website=[[YouTube]]| date=April 13, 2014}}{{cbignore}}</ref> This prompted significant interest in Lehrer's works and helped to secure distribution in Britain for his five-year-old debut album. It was there that his music achieved real sales popularity, as a result of the proliferation of university newspapers referring to the material, and inadvertently due to the [[BBC]], which in 1958 banned from broadcast 10 of the 12 songs on the album.<ref>{{Cite news |date=December 14, 2007 |title=Unfit for Auntie's airwaves: The artists censored by the BBC |language=en |work=The Independent |url=http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/unfit-for-aunties-airwaves-the-artists-censored-by-the-bbc-765106.html |access-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-date=February 2, 2009 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090202175948/http://www.independent.co.uk/arts-entertainment/music/features/unfit-for-aunties-airwaves-the-artists-censored-by-the-bbc-765106.html |url-status=live }}</ref> By the end of the 1950s, Lehrer had sold 370,000 records.<ref name="Smith"/>

===''That Was The Week That Was''===
In 1960, Lehrer essentially retired from touring in the U.S.<ref name="Smith"/> That same year, however, he toured Australia and New Zealand, performing a total of 33 concerts to great acclaim<ref name="Demento"/> and controversy.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Lehrer Dissected … {{!}} NZETC|url=http://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Salient23041960-t1-body-d16-d1.html|access-date=April 6, 2021|website=nzetc.victoria.ac.nz|archive-date=February 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190204190301/http://nzetc.victoria.ac.nz/tm/scholarly/tei-Salient23041960-t1-body-d16-d1.html|url-status=live}}</ref> While in New Zealand, he penned lyrics critical of the [[1960 New Zealand rugby union tour of Australia and South Africa|All Blacks' upcoming tour of Apartheid-era South Africa]] and Prime Minister [[Walter Nash]]'s stance on it.<ref>{{cite news |last1=Berry |first1=John |title="Oh, Mr Nash," says Tom Lehrer |work=Auckland Star |date=April 16, 1960}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |last1=Berry |first1=John |title=Seeing Stars - A Study of Show Folk in New Zealand |date=1964 |publisher=Seven Seas |location=Wellington |pages=75–78}}</ref> Lehrer's tours occurred during a time in which he was, he said, "banned, censored, mentioned in several houses of parliament and threatened with arrest." In particular, "Be Prepared" drew advance resistance in [[Brisbane]] from the commissioner of police. He performed several songs in Australia that were still unreleased, including "The Masochism Tango."<ref name="SMH"/> 

In the early 1960s, Lehrer was employed as the resident songwriter for the U.S. edition of ''[[That Was The Week That Was#US versions|That Was The Week That Was]]'' (TW3), a satirical television show.<ref name="Demento"/> A greater proportion of his output became overtly political, or at least topical, on subjects such as education ("[[New Math (song)|New Math]]"), the [[Second Vatican Council]] ("[[The Vatican Rag]]"), race relations ("National Brotherhood Week"), air and water pollution ("Pollution"<ref name="cbc/player/9.6847426">{{cite web |title=Tom Lehrer performs 'Pollution' on 'The Public Eye' |url=https://www.cbc.ca/player/play/video/9.6847426 |website=[[Canadian Broadcasting Corporation]] |access-date=1 August 2025 |quote=The satirical songwriter plays "Pollution" from his 1965 album "That Was The Year That Was." Aired Jan. 4, 1966 on CBC's The Public Eye.}}</ref>), American militarism ("Send the Marines"), and [[nuclear proliferation]] ("Who's Next?" and "[[Multilateral Force|MLF]] Lullaby"). He also wrote a song satirizing rocket scientist [[Wernher von Braun]], who worked for [[Nazi Germany]] before working for the United States. Lehrer did not appear on TW3; vocalist [[Nancy Ames]] performed his songs (to Lehrer's chagrin),<ref name="Crazy College"/> and lines were often cut from his songs.<ref name="Crazy College"/> Lehrer later performed nine of these songs at the [[Hungry i]] nightclub in [[San Francisco]], and this became the album ''[[That Was the Year That Was]]'' (1965).<ref name="Morris"/>

In 1966, BBC TV host [[David Frost]] returned to the UK with the BBC program ''[[The Frost Report]]''; alongside [[Julie Felix]], Lehrer provided musical satire on the weekly subject.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.bbc.co.uk/comedy/thefrostreport/|title=The Frost Report|publisher=BBC Comedy|access-date=May 9, 2023|archive-date=April 15, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230415033653/https://www.bbc.co.uk/comedy/thefrostreport/|url-status=dead}}</ref> The show was transmitted live, and he pre-recorded all his segments at one performance.<ref name="Morris">{{cite web|last = Morris|first = Jeff|title = Tom Lehrer Discography|publisher = Demented Music Database (dmdb.org)|url = http://dmdb.org/discographies/lehrer.disco.html|access-date = May 8, 2023|archive-date = May 8, 2023|archive-url = https://web.archive.org/web/20230508111019/http://dmdb.org/discographies/lehrer.disco.html|url-status = live}}</ref> Lehrer was not featured in every edition, but his songs featured in an appropriate part of each show.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.theofficialmartyfeldman.com/main/news/marty-meets-tom/|title=Marty meets Tom|date=January 18, 2016|publisher=The Official Marty Feldman|access-date=May 8, 2023|archive-date=May 8, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230508120107/http://www.theofficialmartyfeldman.com/main/news/marty-meets-tom/|url-status=dead}}</ref> At least two of these songs were not included on any of his LPs: a reworking of [[Noël Coward]]'s "That is the End of the News" (with some new lyrics)<ref>{{Citation |title=The end of the news .. heh .wmv | date=May 25, 2011 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lto81YU2Nj4 |language=en |access-date=December 23, 2022 |archive-date=December 23, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223081414/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=lto81YU2Nj4 |url-status=live }}</ref> and a comic explanation of how Britain might adapt to the [[Decimal Day|coming of decimal currency]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ntW9NDRHXnc |title=Lehrer Decimal The Frost Report - YouTube |website=[[YouTube]] |date=July 8, 2013 |access-date=December 23, 2022 |archive-date=December 23, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221223103943/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ntW9NDRHXnc |url-status=live }}</ref> 

Lehrer's record deal with [[Reprise Records]] for ''That Was The Year That Was'' also gave Reprise distribution rights for his earlier recordings, because Lehrer wanted to [[Liquidation|wind up]] his own record imprint.<ref name="Crazy College"/> The Reprise issue of ''Songs by Tom Lehrer'' was a stereo re-recording. This version was not issued on CD, as Lehrer was unhappy with this version.<ref name="Morris"/> The live recording included bonus tracks "L-Y" and "Silent E", two of the ten songs that he wrote for the [[PBS]] children's educational series ''[[The Electric Company (1971 TV series)|The Electric Company]]''. Lehrer later commented that worldwide sales of the recordings under Reprise surpassed 1.8 million units in 1996. That same year, ''That Was The Year That Was'' went gold.<ref name="Bessman"/> The album [[liner notes]] promote his songs with self-deprecating humor, such as quoting a ''[[New York Times]]'' review from 1959: Mr. Lehrer's muse is "not fettered by such inhibiting factors as taste".<ref>{{Cite news |last=Wilson |first=J. S. |author-link=John S. Wilson (music critic) |date=February 9, 1959 |title=Tom Lehrer in Program; Offers His Brand of 'Sick' Humor at Town Hall |language=en-US |work=The New York Times |url=https://www.nytimes.com/1959/02/09/archives/tom-lehrer-in-program-offers-his-brand-of-sick-humor-at-town-hall.html |access-date=October 22, 2020 |issn=0362-4331 |archive-date=October 26, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201026061902/https://www.nytimes.com/1959/02/09/archives/tom-lehrer-in-program-offers-his-brand-of-sick-humor-at-town-hall.html |url-status=live }}</ref>

Lehrer toured Sweden, Norway, and Denmark in 1967;<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/songs%20by%20tom%20lehrer.pdf|author=Ronald L. Smith |title=Songs by Tom Lehrer|publisher=LOC.gov|access-date=May 8, 2023|archive-date=May 22, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230522064135/https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/songs%20by%20tom%20lehrer.pdf|url-status=live}}</ref> his concert in Oslo was recorded for Danish television and subsequently released on DVD some 40 years later.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://premiereoperaintl.com/dvd16802tomlehrerlivefromoslo.aspx|title=Premiere Opera|access-date=November 13, 2020|archive-date=November 14, 2020|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201114124755/https://premiereoperaintl.com/dvd16802tomlehrerlivefromoslo.aspx|url-status=live}}</ref> He performed as a prominent international guest at the ''Studenterforeningen'' (student association) in Copenhagen, which was televised, and he commented on stage that he might be America's "revenge for [[Victor Borge]]".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.youtube.com/6funswede |title=The Tom Lehrer Wisdom Channel |publisher=YouTube |date=September 11, 1967 |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=June 28, 2013 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130628092336/http://www.youtube.com/6funswede |url-status=live }}</ref> He performed original songs in a [[Dodge]] automobile industrial film distributed primarily to automobile dealers and shown at promotional events in 1967, set in a fictional American wild west town and titled ''The Dodge Rebellion Theatre presents Ballads For '67''.<ref name="Demento"/><ref>{{cite web|title=The Dodge industrial film|url=http://home.broadpark.no/~emeyn/tl/dodge.html|website=The Tom Lehrer Wisdom Channel|access-date=March 21, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170420112540/http://home.broadpark.no/~emeyn/tl/dodge.html|archive-date=April 20, 2017|url-status=dead}}</ref> He attempted to adapt ''[[Sweeney Todd]]'' as a Broadway musical, working with [[Joe Raposo]], to star [[Jerry Colonna (entertainer)|Jerry Colonna]]. They started a few songs but, as Lehrer noted, "Nothing ever came of it, and of course twenty years later [[Stephen Sondheim]] [[Sweeney Todd: The Demon Barber of Fleet Street|beat me to the punch]]."<ref>{{cite book|last1=Nachman|first1=Gerald|title=Seriously funny the rebel comedians of the 1950s and 1960s|date=2003|publisher=Pantheon Books|location=New York|isbn=978-0307490728|page=149|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=45tG8jqrx5oC&pg=PA149|access-date=September 11, 2016|archive-date=August 17, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210817202331/https://books.google.com/books?id=45tG8jqrx5oC&pg=PA149|url-status=live}}</ref>

===Departure from the music scene===
{{Infobox
| above            = L-Y

}}

Although Lehrer was "a hero of the [[Anti-nuclear movement|anti-nuclear]], [[Civil rights movement|civil rights]] [[Left-wing politics|left]]", he disliked the aesthetics of the [[counterculture of the 1960s]] and largely stopped performing in the United States as the movement gained momentum.<ref name="Smith" />

In the 1970s, Lehrer concentrated on teaching mathematics and musical theater,<ref name="Severo">{{Cite news |first1=Richard |last1=Severo |first2=Peter |last2=Keepnews |date=July 27, 2025 |title=Tom Lehrer, Musical Satirist With a Dark Streak, Dies at 97 |work=[[The New York Times]] |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/27/arts/music/tom-lehrer-dead.html |access-date=July 27, 2025 |language=en-US |archive-date=July 27, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727170857/https://www.nytimes.com/2025/07/27/arts/music/tom-lehrer-dead.html |url-status=live }}</ref> although he also wrote ten songs for the educational children's television show ''[[The Electric Company]]''. His last public performance for many years took place in 1972, on a fundraising tour for the [[anti-Vietnam War]] Democratic U.S. presidential candidate [[George McGovern]].<ref name="Smith"/><ref name="Bernstein"/>

When asked why he had abandoned his musical career in an interview for the booklet accompanying his CD boxed set, ''[[The Remains of Tom Lehrer]]'' (2000), Lehrer replied: "If an idea came to me, I'd write, and if it didn't I wouldn't&mdash;and, gradually, the second option prevailed over the first. Occasionally people ask 'If you enjoyed it'&mdash;and I did&mdash;'why don't you do it again?' I reply, 'I enjoyed high school but I certainly wouldn't want to do ''that'' again.{{'"}}<ref>[[Dr. Demento]], 2000, ''Too Many Facts About Tom Lehrer'', p. 15. Rhino Entertainment Company</ref> 

Yet at different times he gave other explanations for quitting. In 1973, he had said that "[[political satire]] became obsolete when [[Henry Kissinger]] was awarded the [[Nobel Peace Prize]]."<ref name="Crimson">{{cite web |last1=Gao |first1=Sophie |last2=Silverman |first2=Sarah F. |date=August 2, 2025 |title=Tom Lehrer '47, Mathematician and Musician Who Set Wicked Satire to Cheery Tunes, Dies at 97 |url=https://www.thecrimson.com/article/2025/8/2/tom-lehrer-obituary/ |publisher=[[Harvard University]] |work=[[The Harvard Crimson]] |access-date=September 6, 2025}}</ref> He later stated, in an interview with ''[[The A.V. Club]]'' in 2000, that this was only an off-hand remark and was not the actual reason for him quitting.<ref>{{cite interview |last=Lehrer |first=Tom  |subject-link=Tom Lehrer |date=May 24, 2000 |title=Tom Lehrer |url=https://www.avclub.com/tom-lehrer-1798208112 |work=[[The Onion A.V. Club]] |interviewer-last=Thompson  |interviewer-first=Stephen |interviewer-link=Stephen Thompson (journalist) |access-date= May 6, 2026}}</ref> In 1981, at a New York performance of ''[[Tomfoolery (musical)|Tomfoolery]]'', he told ''[[The New York Times]]'', "The Vietnam War is what changed it. Everybody got earnest. My purpose was to make people laugh and not applaud. If the audience applauds they’re just showing they agree with me. But that’s not humor. So I dropped out just in time."<ref name="Crimson" /><ref>{{cite news| first= Todd S.| last= Purdom| url= https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2000/jul/31/artsfeatures1| title= 'When Kissinger won the Nobel peace prize, satire died'| work= The Guardian| date= July 31, 2000| publisher= | access-date= | archive-date= December 8, 2023| archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20231208040151/https://www.theguardian.com/culture/2000/jul/31/artsfeatures1| url-status= live}}</ref>

Lehrer's musical career was relatively brief. He once mentioned that he performed a mere 109 shows and wrote 37 songs over 20 years.<ref>{{cite web |last=Andrews |first=Dale |url=https://www.sleuthsayers.org/search/label/Tom%20Lehrer |title=Tom Lehrer |publisher=SleuthSayers |date=April 9, 2013 |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924102735/http://www.sleuthsayers.org/search/label/Tom%20Lehrer |url-status=live }}</ref> Nevertheless, he developed a cult following in subsequent decades.<ref>{{Cite magazine |last=Kreps |first=Daniel |date=July 27, 2025 |title=Tom Lehrer, Influential Song Satirist With a Cult Following, Dead at 97 |url=https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/tom-lehrer-song-satirist-dead-obit-1235394850/ |access-date=July 28, 2025 |magazine=Rolling Stone |language=en-US |archive-date=July 27, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250727230114/https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/tom-lehrer-song-satirist-dead-obit-1235394850/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

===Revivals and reissues===
[[File:Portrait of Tom Lehrer in c. 1983 (retouched).jpg|thumb|left|upright|Lehrer {{circa|1983}}]]
Lehrer's music became a staple of ''The [[Doctor Demento]] Show'' when it began national syndication in 1977.<ref>{{cite magazine| magazine= [[Billboard (magazine)|Billboard]]| title= Lehrer| page= 19| date= July 10, 1982| volume= 94| number= 27 |issn= 0006-2510}}</ref> In 1980, [[Cameron Mackintosh]] produced ''[[Tomfoolery (musical)|Tomfoolery]]'', a revue of Lehrer's songs that was a hit on the London stage. Lehrer was not initially involved with the show, but he was pleased with it; he eventually gave the stage production his full support and updated several of his lyrics for the show. ''Tomfoolery'' contained 27 songs and led to more than 200 productions,<ref name="Bessman"/> including an [[Off-Broadway]] production at the [[Village Gate]] which ran for 120 performances in 1981.<ref>{{iobdb title|2186|Tomfoolery}}</ref> Lehrer made a rare TV appearance on [[BBC]]'s ''[[Parkinson (TV series)|Parkinson]]'' show in conjunction with the ''Tomfoolery'' premiere in 1980 at the [[Criterion Theatre]] in London, where he sang "I Got It from Agnes".<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/43413/tom-lehrer-collection-cd-dvd-the/ |title=The Tom Lehrer Collection (CD + DVD) : DVD Talk Review of the DVD Video |publisher=| website= dvdtalk.com |access-date=October 27, 2015 |archive-date=September 24, 2015 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150924044309/http://www.dvdtalk.com/reviews/43413/tom-lehrer-collection-cd-dvd-the/ |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{YouTube|EDeRYmB4t6Q|Tom Lehrer: I Got It From Agnes}}—from "Parkinson" 1980</ref> There were ''Tomfoolery'' performances in San Francisco about 1982 and in 2018–19. ''Tomfoolery'' was performed at the [[Arena Stage]] Theater in Washington, DC, in 1982.<ref>{{Cite news |last=Lehrer |first=Tom |date=January 3, 1982 |title=Tom Lehrer: Live & Off-color |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1982/01/03/tom-lehrer-live-38/079cd514-2b53-4183-a6d0-bcef22696a9b/ |newspaper=The Washington Post |language=en-US |issn=0190-8286 |access-date=May 18, 2025 |archive-date=May 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250512071513/https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/lifestyle/style/1982/01/03/tom-lehrer-live-38/079cd514-2b53-4183-a6d0-bcef22696a9b/ |url-status=live }}</ref> In 1993, he wrote "That's Mathematics" for the closing credits to a [[Mathematical Sciences Research Institute]] video<ref>{{cite web|title=Fermat's Last Theorem - The Theorem and Its Proof: An Exploration of Issues and Ideas|url=http://videodl.msri.org/data/000/022/041/original/fermat-fermat-QuickTime.mov |website=MSRI.org |publisher=Mathematical Sciences Research Institute|location=Palace of Fine Arts, San Francisco |date= July 28, 1993 |archive-date=August 9, 2016|archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160809100706/http://videodl.msri.org/data/000/022/041/original/fermat-fermat-QuickTime.mov|url-status= live |access-date=April 7, 2017}}</ref> celebrating the proof of [[Fermat's Last Theorem]].

On June 7 and 8, 1998, Lehrer performed in public for the first time in 18 years at the [[Lyceum Theatre, London]], as part of the show ''[[Hey, Mr. Producer!]]'' celebrating the career of Cameron Mackintosh, who had produced ''Tomfoolery''. The June 8 show was his only performance before Queen [[Elizabeth II]]. Lehrer sang "Poisoning Pigeons in the Park" and an updated version of the nuclear proliferation song "Who's Next?".<ref>{{YouTube|hf-eIgFJg4w|Tom Lehrer - Poisoning Pigeons In The Park (live, 1998).}}</ref>

In 2000, Lehrer commented that he doubted his songs had any real effect on those not already critical of the establishment: "I don't think this kind of thing has an impact on the unconverted, frankly. It's not even preaching to the converted; it's titillating the converted&nbsp;... I'm fond of quoting [[Peter Cook]], who talked about the satirical Berlin [[Kabarett]]s of the 1930s, which did so much to stop the rise of [[Hitler]] and prevent the [[Second World War]]."<ref>{{cite web|last=Thompson|first=Stephen|date=May 24, 2000| title= Tom Lehrer Interview · The A.V. Club|url=https://www.avclub.com/tom-lehrer-1798208112| publisher= | website= avclub.com |archive-date= August 29, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170829120231/http://www.avclub.com/tom-lehrer-1798208112| url-status=live |access-date=October 27, 2015}}</ref>

Lehrer said, jokingly, of his musical career: "If, after hearing my songs, just one human being is inspired to say something nasty to a friend, or perhaps to strike a loved one, it will all have been worth the while."<ref name="Liner notes" /> In 2003, Lehrer commented that his particular brand of political satire is more difficult in the modern world: "The real issues I don't think most people touch. The [[Bill Clinton|Clinton]] jokes are all about [[Monica Lewinsky]] and all that stuff and not about the important things, like the fact that he wouldn't ban [[land mines]]&nbsp;... I'm not tempted to write a song about [[George W. Bush]]. I couldn't figure out what sort of song I would write. That's the problem: I don't want to satirize George Bush and his puppeteers, I want to vaporize them."<ref name="SMH" />

In 2000, the boxed CD set ''The Remains of Tom Lehrer'' was released by [[Rhino Entertainment]]. It included live and studio versions of his first two albums, ''That Was The Year That Was'', the songs that he wrote for ''The Electric Company'', some previously unreleased material, and a small hardbound lyrics book with an introduction by [[Dr. Demento]]. In 2010, [[Shout! Factory]] launched a reissue campaign, making Lehrer's out-of-print albums available digitally. The CD/DVD combo ''The Tom Lehrer Collection'' was issued, including his best-known songs, with a DVD featuring an Oslo concert.<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=126189232 |title=Tom Lehrer: '60s Satirist Still Strikes A Chord |publisher= |website= [[NPR]].org |date=April 30, 2010 |archive-date=September 5, 2015 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20150905114821/http://www.npr.org/templates/story/story.php?storyId=126189232 |url-status=live |access-date=October 27, 2015}}</ref>

== Later life and death ==
In a February 2008 phone call, [[Gene Weingarten]] of ''[[The Washington Post]]'' interviewed Lehrer [[Off the record (journalism)|off the record]]. When Weingarten asked if there was anything he could print for the record, Lehrer responded, "Just tell the people that I am voting for [[Barack Obama|Obama]]."<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/discussion/2008/02/05/DI2008020502027.html |title=Chatological Humor: A Tribute to Tom Lehrer |newspaper=[[The Washington Post]] |date=February 12, 2008 |archive-date=January 23, 2016 |archive-url= https://web.archive.org/web/20160123021733/http://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/discussion/2008/02/05/DI2008020502027.html |url-status=live |access-date=October 27, 2015}}</ref>

In 2012, rapper [[2 Chainz]] sampled Lehrer's song "[[The Old Dope Peddler]]" on his debut album, ''[[Based on a T.R.U. Story]]''. In 2013, Lehrer said he was "very proud" to have his song sampled "literally sixty years after I recorded it". Lehrer went on to describe his official response to the request to use his song: "As sole copyright owner of 'The Old Dope Peddler', I grant you motherfuckers permission to do this. Please give my regards to Mr. Chainz, or may I call him 2?"<ref name="BBC 2013-04-06" /><ref>{{cite magazine | last=Prospero | date=October 17, 2017 | title=Who can fill the role of Tom Lehrer today? | magazine=[[The Economist]] | url=https://www.economist.com/blogs/prospero/2017/10/wit | access-date=January 1, 2018 | archive-date=December 1, 2017 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201194530/https://www.economist.com/blogs/prospero/2017/10/wit | url-status=live }}</ref>

In October 2020, Lehrer transferred the music and lyrics for all songs he had ever written into the [[public domain]]:<ref>{{Cite news |last=Sanderson |first=David |date=October 22, 2020 |title=Copyright-busting website is invitation to have a laugh with Tom Lehrer |language=en |work=[[The Times]] |url=https://www.thetimes.com/culture/theatre-dance/article/copyright-busting-website-is-invitation-to-have-a-laugh-with-tom-lehrer-k99b6b9gh |access-date=October 22, 2020 |issn=0140-0460 |archive-date=October 22, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201022101502/https://www.thetimes.co.uk/article/copyright-busting-website-is-invitation-to-have-a-laugh-with-tom-lehrer-k99b6b9gh |url-status=live }}</ref><ref>{{cite news | title=Satirist Tom Lehrer has put his songs into the public domain | first=Justin | last=Ho | work=Marketplace | date=October 21, 2020 | url=https://www.marketplace.org/2020/10/21/satirist-tom-lehrer-put-his-songs-into-public-domain/ | access-date=October 25, 2020 | archive-date=October 24, 2020 | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20201024223019/https://www.marketplace.org/2020/10/21/satirist-tom-lehrer-put-his-songs-into-public-domain/ | url-status=live }}</ref>
{{Blockquote|text=In short, I no longer retain any rights to any of my songs.
So help yourselves, and don’t send me any money.|author=Tom Lehrer}}
In November 2022, Lehrer formally relinquished the [[copyright]] and performing/recording rights on his songs, making all music and lyrics composed by him free for anyone to use, and established a website from which all of his recordings and printable copies of all of his songs could be downloaded.<ref name="Lehrer songs">{{Cite web |url=https://tomlehrersongs.com/ |title=Tom Lehrer Songs |access-date=December 16, 2022 |date=November 1, 2022 |language=en-us |publisher=Tom Lehrer |archive-date=November 1, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221101152524/https://tomlehrersongs.com/ |url-status=live }}</ref> His statement releasing all his works into the public domain concludes with this note: "This website will be shut down at some date in the not too distant future, so if you want to download anything, don't wait too long."<ref name="Lehrer songs" /> {{As of|June 2026}}, the website is still online.<ref name="Severo" />

Comedy label [[Stand Up! Records]] released Lehrer's holiday songs "(I'm Spending) [[Hanukkah]] in [[Santa Monica]]," which he had written for [[Garrison Keillor]]'s ''The American Radio Company of the Air'' in 1990 and recorded later,<ref name="Bianculli" />{{efn|[[David Bianculli]] writes, "The idea was to provide a Jewish counterpart to such Christmas classics as "[[White Christmas (song)|White Christmas]]," and quotes a section: "But in December, there's just one place for me. Amid the California flora, I'll be lighting my menorah. Like a baby in his cradle, I'll be playing with my dreidel. Here's to Judas Maccabeus: Boy, if he could only see us spending Hanukkah in Santa Monica by the sea."<ref name="Bianculli" />}} and "A Christmas Carol" as a seven-inch single in 2024. The limited-edition release also included sheet music for both songs.<ref name="Lobell">{{cite web |url=https://jewishjournal.com/culture/arts/music/376941/stand-up-records-releases-tom-lehrer-vinyl-just-in-time-for-hanukkah/ |title=Stand Up! Records Releases Tom Lehrer Vinyl Just in Time for Hanukkah |last=Lobell |first=Kylie Ora |date=November 20, 2024 |work=[[The Jewish Journal of Greater Los Angeles]]; jewishjournal.com |access-date=April 13, 2025 |archive-date=May 12, 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250512113514/https://jewishjournal.com/culture/arts/music/376941/stand-up-records-releases-tom-lehrer-vinyl-just-in-time-for-hanukkah/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

Lehrer never married and had no children.<ref name="Severo" /><ref>{{Cite web |first1=Ben |last1=Smith |first2=Anita |last2=Badejo |date=2014-04-10 |title=Looking For Tom Lehrer, Comedy's Mysterious Genius |url=https://www.buzzfeed.com/bensmith/tom-lehrer |access-date=2025-07-30 |website=BuzzFeed |language=en |archive-date=November 29, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211129061734/https://www.buzzfeed.com/bensmith/tom-lehrer |url-status=live }}</ref> He died at his home in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on July 26, 2025, at the age of 97.<ref name="Severo" />

==Musical legacy==

In 1967, Swedish actor [[Lars Ekborg]], known outside Sweden for his part in [[Ingmar Bergman]]'s ''[[Summer with Monika]]'', made an album called ''I Tom Lehrers vackra värld'' ("In the beautiful world of Tom Lehrer"), with 12 of Lehrer's songs translated into [[Swedish language|Swedish]]. Lehrer wrote in a letter to the producer {{Interlanguage link|Per-Anders Boquist|sv}} that, "Not knowing any Swedish, I am obviously not equipped to judge, but it sounds to me as though Mr. Ekborg is perfect for the songs", along with further compliments to pianist {{Interlanguage link|Leif Asp|sv}} for unexpected additional flourishes.<ref>Liner notes (translation): {{cite book|last1=Holmgren|first1=Pontus|title=Lars Ekborg i Tom Lehrer's Vackra Värld|date=2002|publisher=Amigo|location=Sweden|url=http://www.tomlehrer.org/covers/ekborgnotes1.html|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150621060642/http://www.tomlehrer.org/covers/ekborgnotes1.html|archive-date=June 21, 2015}}</ref>

In 1971, Argentinian singer [[Nacha Guevara]] sang Spanish versions of several Lehrer songs for the show/live album ''Este es el año que es''.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.tomlehrer.org/covers/guevara.html |title=Nacha Guevara |access-date=September 20, 2023 | website=TomLehrer.org |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150219063342/http://www.tomlehrer.org/covers/guevara.html |archive-date=February 19, 2015 }}</ref><ref>{{cite book|url=https://www.nachaguevaraweb.com/index.php/1971-este-es-el-ano-que-es|title=Este es el año que es|last1=Guevara|first1=Nacha|date=1971|publisher=Music Hall|location=Argentina|access-date=February 26, 2019|archive-date=February 26, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190226111128/https://www.nachaguevaraweb.com/index.php/1971-este-es-el-ano-que-es|url-status=live}} Track list and lyrics (Spanish).</ref> In the 1950s, [[Georg Kreisler]] wrote two songs likely inspired by Tom Lehrer's "Poisoning Pigeons in the Park" and "I Hold Your Hand in Mine", as mentioned by Lehrer himself even though disputed by Kreisler. Composer [[Randy Newman]] said of Lehrer, "He's one of the great American songwriters without a doubt, right up there with everybody, the top guys. As a lyricist, as good as there's been in the last half of the 20th century."<ref name="BBC 2013-04-06" /> Singer and comedian [[Dillie Keane]] has acknowledged Lehrer's influence on her work.<ref>{{cite web|first=Sheila |last=Connor|website=The British Theatre Guide|url=http://www.britishtheatreguide.info/otherresources/interviews/DillieKeane.htm|title=Dillie Keane Interview|access-date=December 24, 2013|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091008023413/http://www.britishtheatreguide.info/otherresources/interviews/DillieKeane.htm|archive-date=October 8, 2009|url-status=dead}}</ref>

[[Dr. Demento]] praised Lehrer as "the best musical satirist of the twentieth century." Other artists who cite Lehrer as an influence include [["Weird Al" Yankovic]], whose work generally addresses more [[pop culture|popular]] and less technical or political subjects,<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.weirdal.com/faq.htm |title=Weird Al's FAQs |author="Weird Al" Yankovic |author-link="Weird Al" Yankovic|website=Weirdal.com |access-date=June 12, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060902235037/http://www.weirdal.com/faq.htm|archive-date=September 2, 2006}}</ref> and educator and scientist [[H. Paul Shuch]], who tours under the stage name Dr. SETI, and calls himself "a cross between [[Carl Sagan]] and Tom Lehrer: He sings like Sagan and lectures like Lehrer."<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.setileague.org/admin/paul.htm|title=SETI League executive director emeritus Dr. H. Paul Shuch|website=Setileague.org|access-date=April 7, 2017|archive-date=April 8, 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170408082650/http://www.setileague.org/admin/paul.htm|url-status=live}}</ref> Yankovic saw [[Daniel Radcliffe]] (who called Lehrer his "hero")<ref>{{Citation |title=Daniel Radcliffe sings "The Elements" - The Graham Norton Show - Series 8 Episode 4 - BBC One | date=November 12, 2010 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rSAaiYKF0cs |language=en |access-date=November 4, 2022 |archive-date=November 3, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103231819/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rSAaiYKF0cs |url-status=live }}</ref> perform "The Elements" on ''[[The Graham Norton Show]]'' in his native United Kingdom,<ref name="youtube/rSAaiYKF0cs">{{cite web |title=Daniel Radcliffe sings "The Elements" |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rSAaiYKF0cs |website=[[The Graham Norton Show]] - [[List_of_The_Graham_Norton_Show_episodes#Series_8_(2010–2011)|Series 8 Episode 4]] |publisher=[[BBC]] |access-date=31 July 2025 |date=12 November 2010 |archive-date=November 3, 2022 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20221103231819/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rSAaiYKF0cs |url-status=live }}</ref> which led to Radcliffe starring in ''[[Weird: The Al Yankovic Story]]''.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/daniel-radcliffe-weird-al-biopic-elements-song-1235115049/|title=Daniel Radcliffe Says He Landed 'Weird Al' Role Due to Novelty Song He Performed for Rihanna|date=March 19, 2022|first=Ryan|last=Gajewski|website=[[The Hollywood Reporter]]|access-date=September 21, 2023|archive-date=May 13, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220513065720/https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/tv/tv-news/daniel-radcliffe-weird-al-biopic-elements-song-1235115049/|url-status=live}}</ref>

From January 16 to February 25, 2006, the play ''[[Letters from Lehrer]]'', written and performed by Canadian [[Richard Greenblatt (playwright)|Richard Greenblatt]], ran at [[Canadian Stage Company|CanStage]] in Toronto. It followed Lehrer's musical career, the meaning of several songs, the politics of the time, and Greenblatt's own experiences with Lehrer's music, while playing some of Lehrer's songs.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Ouzounian|first=Richard|date=January 29, 2006|title=Letters From Lehrer|url=https://variety.com/2006/legit/reviews/letters-from-lehrer-1200518948/|access-date=November 11, 2021|website=Variety|language=en-US|archive-date=November 11, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211111164139/https://variety.com/2006/legit/reviews/letters-from-lehrer-1200518948/|url-status=live}}</ref>

In the March 16, 2006, issue of [[New York (magazine)|''New York'' magazine]], [[Donald Fagen]] of [[Steely Dan]] named Tom Lehrer among the writers who had influenced him and his songwriting partner [[Walter Becker]]. "We also liked comic songwriting, like Tom Lehrer. He was a piano player and songwriter who wrote these grim, funny songs."<ref>{{Cite news |url=https://nymag.com/arts/popmusic/profiles/16453/ |title=Influences: Donald Fagen |author=Williams, Ben |work=New York Magazine |date=March 16, 2006 |access-date=June 30, 2023 |archive-date=June 30, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230630221931/https://nymag.com/arts/popmusic/profiles/16453/ |url-status=live }}</ref>

In 2010, the German musician-comedian {{Interlanguage link|Felix Janosa|de}} released an album with the title ''Tauben vergiften: Die bösen Lieder von Tom Lehrer'' ("Poisoning pigeons: The Evil Songs of Tom Lehrer"), with German versions of some of his best-known songs.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Tauben vergiften - Die bösen Lieder des Tom Lehrer - Felix Janosa|website=AllMusic|url=https://www.allmusic.com/album/tauben-vergiften-die-b%C3%B6sen-lieder-des-tom-lehrer-mw0002570106|language=en|access-date=November 11, 2021|archive-date=November 11, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211111164139/https://www.allmusic.com/album/tauben-vergiften-die-b%C3%B6sen-lieder-des-tom-lehrer-mw0002570106|url-status=live}}</ref>

In 2024, [[Francis Beckett]] wrote a play ''Tom Lehrer Is Teaching Math and Doesn't Want to Talk to You'', which features Lehrer's music and was performed with Lehrer's tacit approval at the [[Upstairs at The Gatehouse]] theatre in [[Highgate, London]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.theguardian.com/music/article/2024/may/22/my-songs-spread-like-herpes-why-did-satirical-genius-tom-lehrer-swap-worldwide-fame-for-obscurity|title=My songs spread like herpes, why did satirical genius Tom Lehrer swap worldwide fame for obscurity|author=Beckett, Francis |work=[[The Guardian]] |date = May 22, 2024|access-date=May 30, 2024}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.londontheatre1.com/reviews/tom-lehrer-is-teaching-math-and-doesnt-want-to-talk-to-you-review/ |last=O'Brien |first=John |date=May 30, 2024 |title=Tom Lehrer is Teaching Math and Doesn't Want to Talk to You |access-date=May 31, 2024 |website=LondonTheatre1 |archive-date=May 30, 2024 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20240530203620/https://www.londontheatre1.com/reviews/tom-lehrer-is-teaching-math-and-doesnt-want-to-talk-to-you-review/ |url-status=live }}</ref>
[[File:The Physical Revue (1952).webp|thumb|Lehrer at the piano during The Physical Revue, c. 1952]]
In 2025, ''[[The Harvard Crimson]]'' recalls how Lehrer expressed his surprise that "well, I wrote 'Fight Fiercely, Harvard' in 1945" and it was still being performed in the 21st century. ''The Crimson'' comments, "[As] [[Harvard University#Second presidency of Donald Trump|Harvard squares off]] with the [[Second presidency of Donald Trump|Trump administration]], the song — which genteelly urges football players to 'hurl that spheroid down the field' — has become a [[Protest song|protest anthem]] of sorts, too."<ref name="Crimson" /> 

Performers influenced by Lehrer's style include American political satirist [[Mark Russell]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.holecity.com/asp/newshole.asp?issue=10&sec=7&hole=1 |title=NewsHole |publisher=Holecity.com |date=March 5, 2000 |access-date=June 12, 2009 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20071013212746/http://holecity.com/asp/newshole.asp?issue=10&sec=7&hole=1 |archive-date=October 13, 2007 }}</ref> Canadian comedian and songwriter [[Randy Vancourt]], and the British duo Kit and The Widow. Composer/cabarettist [[Leonard Lehrman]] extended three of Lehrer's songs, writing a new verse 4 to "Clementine",<ref>{{Citation|title=20230311 20 Clementine| date=March 25, 2023 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spO4TPdE9bg|language=en|access-date=April 30, 2023|archive-date=May 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230501030257/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=spO4TPdE9bg&gl=US&hl=en|url-status=live}}</ref> a new verse 2 to "Hanukkah in Santa Monica",<ref>{{Citation|title=20170409 07 Hanukka in SantaMonica + GootYuntif| date=April 15, 2017 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iWuuBO7DWwk|language=en|access-date=April 30, 2023|archive-date=May 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230501030247/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iWuuBO7DWwk|url-status=live}}</ref> and a new verse 3 to "The Elements".<ref>{{Citation|title=04+202100601 The Elements Updated (2021)| date=June 2, 2021 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKtpaHqP6ig|language=en|access-date=April 30, 2023|archive-date=May 1, 2023|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20230501030244/https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MKtpaHqP6ig|url-status=live}}</ref>

Lehrer has been referred to as the "King of Satire" by fans.<ref>{{Cite book |last=Porter |first=Zeth J. "Bishop" |title=The Fate of the King: A Study of Tom Lehrer |publisher=Brainy Books |date=March 26, 2023 |location=Tomball, TX |page=8 |language=en}}</ref>

==Publications==
'''Mathematics'''

*{{cite web |last1=Fagen |first1=R. E |last2=Lehrer |first2=T. A. |title=The Gambler's Ruin with Soft-Hearted Adversary (Random Walks with Restraining Barrier and Absorbing Barrier)|url=https://www.nsa.gov/portals/75/documents/news-features/declassified-documents/gamblers-ruin.pdf<!--   copy  https://media.defense.gov/2021/Jul/14/2002762807/-1/-1/0/GAMBLERS-RUIN.PDF/GAMBLERS-RUIN.PDF --> |publisher=[[National Security Agency]] |date=24 January 1957}}
::see: [[gambler's ruin]].  Contains a reference to a fictional mathematical paper, quoted from the lyrics to his song [[Lobachevsky (song)|Lobachevsky]]: ''Analytic and Algebraic Topology of Locally Euclidean Metrizations of Infinitely Differentiable Riemannian Manifolds''.  The NSA paper was later edited and published by [[American Mathematical Society]] in March 1958, complete with fictional reference.<ref name="AMSobit">{{Cite web|url=https://www.ams.org/journals/notices/202602/noti3297/noti3297.html|title=AMS :: Notices of the American Mathematical Society|website=Ams.org|access-date=April 9, 2026}}</ref>

The [[American Mathematical Society]] database lists him as co-author of two papers:

* {{Cite journal |last1=Fagen |first1=R. E |last2=Lehrer |first2=T. A. |title=Random Walks with Restraining Barrier as Applied to the Biased Binary Counter |journal=[[Journal of the Society for Industrial and Applied Mathematics]] |volume=6 |number=1 |date=March 1958 |pages=1–14 |doi=10.1137/0106001 |jstor=2098858 |mr=0094856 |ref=none}}
* {{Cite journal |author1=T. Austin |author2=R. Fagen |author3=T. Lehrer |author4= W. Penney |date=September 1957 |title=The Distribution of the Number of Locally Maximal Elements in a Random Sample |journal=[[Annals of Mathematical Statistics]] |volume=28 |number=3 |pages=786–790 |doi=10.1214/aoms/1177706893 |mr=0091251 |doi-access=free |ref=none}}

'''Songs'''

Two of Lehrer's songs were reprinted, with his permission, in [[Mad (magazine)|''Mad'' magazine]]:<ref>{{Cite web|title=Doug Gilford's Mad Cover Site - Mad Magazine Contributors - Master List|url=https://madcoversite.com/ugoi-master.html#tom_lehrer|access-date=December 21, 2021|website=madcoversite.com|archive-date=December 21, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211221164227/https://madcoversite.com/ugoi-master.html#tom_lehrer|url-status=live}}</ref>

* "Tom Lehrer Sings 'The Wild West Is Where I Want to Be{{'"}} (illustrated by [[George Woodbridge (illustrator)|George Woodbridge]], ''MAD'' 32, April 1957)<ref>{{Cite web|title=Doug Gilford's Mad Cover Site - Mad 32|url=https://madcoversite.com/mad032.html|access-date=December 21, 2021|website=madcoversite.com|archive-date=November 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211116030622/https://www.madcoversite.com/mad032.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
* "Tom Lehrer's 'The Hunting Song{{'"}} (illustrated by George Woodbridge, ''MAD'' 35, October 1957)<ref>{{Cite web|title=Doug Gilford's Mad Cover Site - Mad 35|url=https://madcoversite.com/mad035.html|access-date=December 21, 2021|website=madcoversite.com|archive-date=November 16, 2021|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211116030629/https://www.madcoversite.com/mad035.html|url-status=live}}</ref>
